Pregnancy

Cold symptoms in pregnancy: why herbal steam is not the best remedy

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A pregnancy cold can make home remedies tempting, especially when you are unsure which medicines are suitable. The useful next step is a safe symptom plan: not choosing the strongest-smelling steam mixture.

A cold is uncomfortable, but not every respiratory illness is the same

A blocked or runny nose, sore throat and cough can make pregnancy tiring. An uncomplicated common cold is usually mild and settles with time. Pregnancy changes immune, respiratory and circulatory function, but describing the whole immune system as simply switched down to stop it attacking the baby is too simplistic. It does not mean every pregnant person is destined to catch repeated infections.

Influenza and some other respiratory illnesses can be more serious during pregnancy. Sudden fever, marked body aches or feeling unusually ill deserves medical advice rather than the assumption that it is just a cold. Fever should be assessed and managed appropriately. Drinking water helps prevent dehydration, but it is not a substitute for evaluating a significant fever or treating an illness that needs treatment.

Rest, fluids and ordinary food are useful foundations

Make room for rest when you are tired or achy, and ask for help with tasks if possible. Drink regularly to avoid dehydration, using smaller amounts more often if nausea makes drinking difficult. You do not need to force very large volumes. Contact your care team if you cannot keep fluids down, are passing much less urine or feel faint.

Continue eating what you can tolerate. Fruit and vegetables such as citrus, strawberries, mango, tomatoes, peppers, cabbage-family vegetables and spinach contribute nutrients, including vitamin C in varying amounts; watermelon can also be part of your food and fluid intake. These foods support a varied diet, but none acts as a proven cold cure or needs to be eaten in a prescribed quantity.

Keep supplements and throat care in proportion

Continue the pregnancy supplements recommended for you, rather than adding several immune-boosting products. There is little evidence that starting vitamin C, garlic or similar supplements treats a cold quickly, and excessive or combined doses can create separate problems. Check any new vitamin, herb or cold remedy with a pharmacist or clinician who knows you are pregnant.

For an adult sore throat, a warm saltwater gargle may soothe discomfort: dissolve about half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, gargle and spit it out. Do not swallow it or use scalding water. A comfortably warm drink may also help. These are comfort measures, not ways to kill all respiratory viruses or replace care for worsening symptoms.

Why a bowl of steam is not the best next step

Steam inhalation usually means leaning over hot water, sometimes under a towel, with herbs or oils added. A warm sensation may feel temporarily relieving, but there is no strong evidence that this speeds recovery from a cold. The bowl can tip suddenly and cause serious scalds to the face, chest or legs. Avoid this method rather than trying to make it safer by choosing a different herb.

Plain saline nasal spray is a simpler option to ask about for congestion. A normal comfortably warm shower is different from bending over boiling water, but it should not become a prolonged overheating session. If you use a humidifier, follow its cleaning instructions. Do not add essential oils or baking soda to a humidifier, nebulizer or other breathing device unless the device and your clinician specifically direct it.

Pennyroyal is not a reassuring pregnancy remedy

Pennyroyal and related mint names appear in traditional remedies for headache, fever, congestion, mucus and sore throat. A common plant name may refer to different species or preparations. Claims that the vapour disinfects a room, prevents transmission or is safe because no serious reaction has been reported do not establish either effectiveness or pregnancy safety.

Pennyroyal oil is a concentrated product with documented severe poisoning after ingestion, including liver failure and death. That evidence must not be misrepresented as a measured inhalation risk, but it certainly does not provide a safe steam recipe. Do not swallow it or use an improvised medicinal preparation. If oil has been swallowed, contact a poison centre or emergency service immediately and do not wait for symptoms.

Eucalyptus and peppermint need product-specific caution

Eucalyptus preparations are marketed for cough, mucus and a blocked nose, but the plant, an essential oil and a finished medicine are not equivalent. Evidence does not justify a universal claim that every eucalyptus inhalation causes high blood pressure in pregnancy, nor does it establish that a homemade concentrated-oil mixture is safe. Have the exact product and route checked instead of relying on either blanket reassurance or a single alarming mechanism.

Peppermint also has different uses and formulations. Familiar flavouring amounts in food are not the same exposure as concentrated oil or repeated medicinal inhalation. Available research does not prove a pregnancy cold benefit for a homemade peppermint steam. Scented vapours can be unpleasant or irritating, particularly for someone with sensitive airways. If a product causes wheezing, breathlessness or worsening symptoms, stop using it and seek appropriate advice.

Baking soda vapour does not treat a respiratory virus

Baking soda inhalation became popular in some home-remedy discussions during COVID-19. Claims that it disinfects airways, destroys viruses or reliably relieves breathlessness are not established treatment advice. There is no validated pregnancy recipe or short exposure time that can be recommended as a safe, effective remedy.

Do not improvise a bowl treatment, inhale powder or put a kitchen mixture into a nebulizer. Breathlessness needs assessment, especially during pregnancy; trying a home inhalation can delay that care. The concern is not that every incidental household exposure has been shown to harm a pregnancy. It is that an unproven inhaled treatment should not be promoted in place of suitable care.

You can ask about medicines instead of avoiding all treatment

Pregnancy-compatible symptom treatment exists. Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, can be used for pain or fever when appropriate and taken as directed. Check the actual product, dose and other medicines with a pharmacist if unsure. Many cold-and-flu combinations contain more than one active ingredient, including duplicate pain relief or a decongestant.

Do not self-start ibuprofen or decongestant tablets, drops or sprays during pregnancy. Advice depends on the ingredient and your circumstances, and current UKTIS guidance advises avoiding these for self-treatment of colds. A plain saline spray is different from a medicated decongestant. Antibiotics do not treat an ordinary viral cold, but a clinician may prescribe medicine for another diagnosis. Necessary care should not be delayed simply because you are pregnant.

Know when to call and how to reduce spread

Contact your maternity or primary-care team promptly if you think you have flu, have a concerning fever, or feel much more unwell than with a usual cold. Antiviral treatment may be recommended for suspected influenza without waiting for test confirmation. It works best when started early, but passing forty-eight hours does not mean you should give up seeking treatment.

Breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion, severe dehydration or collapse needs urgent or emergency help. Contact maternity care for reduced fetal movements once movements are established. Worsening after initial improvement also deserves review. Handwashing, tissues, ventilation and avoiding close contact while unwell are more dependable ways to reduce spread than scenting the room with herbs. Keep recommended pregnancy vaccinations up to date with your care team.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Avoid hot-water bowls for steam inhalation because of scald risk and uncertain benefit.

Herbal names do not identify a standardized product or a safe pregnancy dose.

Suspected flu in pregnancy needs prompt clinical advice.

How BeMama can help

Keep the labels of any remedies you are considering and ask a pharmacist to check their ingredients. Plan rest and help with daily tasks while you recover.

When to seek help

Seek urgent help for breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion, severe dehydration or collapse. Contact a poison centre immediately after swallowing a potentially toxic essential oil.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Rest, fluids and varied food support recovery without promising a cure.
  • Do not treat breathing problems with homemade inhalations.
  • Food flavourings and concentrated oils are different exposures.
  • Pregnancy is not a reason to avoid all medicine or delay needed care.

Frequently asked questions

Which herbal steam is best in pregnancy?

No homemade mixture can be recommended as a proven, risk-free cold treatment. Avoid hot-water bowls and ask about simpler symptom care.

Is pregnancy just a state of weak immunity?

No. Immune and other body systems change in complex ways. Some infections, including flu, can carry greater risk without every ordinary cold being dangerous.

Will vitamin C-rich food cure a cold?

It supports a varied diet, but it is not a proven cure. Do not add high-dose supplements without checking pregnancy suitability.

Can I gargle salt water?

Adults can use comfortably warm salt water for throat comfort and spit it out. It does not replace assessment for a severe or worsening illness.

Is pennyroyal safe because it is a mint?

No. Common names and natural origin are not safety evidence. Concentrated pennyroyal oil can be highly poisonous when swallowed.

Does eucalyptus always raise blood pressure in pregnancy?

That universal claim is not established. It also does not mean improvised eucalyptus-oil inhalation is safe; check the exact product with a clinician or pharmacist.

Must I avoid every food containing peppermint?

Ordinary flavouring amounts differ from medicinal oils. Limited pregnancy information about a concentrated remedy should not be turned into a blanket food ban.

Can baking soda vapour kill a cold or COVID virus?

There is no established clinical basis for that treatment. Do not put kitchen mixtures in breathing equipment or delay care for breathlessness.

Can I take anything for a fever?

Paracetamol may be appropriate when used as directed. Check combination products and get medical advice for a concerning fever or suspected flu.

Is it too late to call about flu after two days?

No. Early treatment is best, but pregnancy is a reason for prompt advice even after forty-eight hours. A clinician can still decide whether treatment is needed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
